clue.text: There's opening to nick lags with dragnet cast around here

definitions.text: There's opening to nick lags with dragnet cast around here

indicators.note: to cast is to throw or mould, so the gathered letters are thrown into a new shape
an opening is the start, so only the first letter of the following word is kept

parts.note: first letter of nick
taken as written; lags are old convicts
taken as written

explanation.surface: A police sweep through a criminal district, nabbing old lags with a net.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well as the wordplay: a district where you might nick lags with a dragnet is the criminal world.
explanation.definitionFit: The criminal underworld is where convicts and crooks congregate, the natural place to throw a police net.

clue.text: What was rank and ranker when picked up? Aussie bug

parts.note: an obsolete word for rank or degree; 'What was' flags the old usage
n is a short form of and, as in rock 'n' roll

indicators.note: picked up means caught by the ear, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: ranker means more gross, said aloud

explanation.surface: A riddle about something that once was rank and grew ranker, answered by an Australian insect.
explanation.walkthrough: Rank looks like a noun for a soldier, but it is an old word meaning degree; ranker is the comparative of rank meaning gross.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australia the common green cicada is popularly called by this shopkeeper's name.

clue.text: Web designers earn a smashing wage on a regular basis

parts.note: taken as written

parts.note: second and fourth letters of wage

explanation.walkthrough: Web designers sounds like internet professionals, but it means the spiders that spin webs.
explanation.definitionFit: The zoological order of spiders, creatures that construct webs, bears this Latin name.

clue.text: Bard's merry old poem recalled after new one

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
I is the Roman numeral one

parts.note: dit is an archaic word for a ditty or poem

explanation.surface: A cheerful old poem by Shakespeare, remembered after a newer one.
explanation.walkthrough: Bard's marks the definition as a poetic, literary word rather than everyday English.
explanation.definitionFit: This rare poetic adjective means shining or bright, and in the gay, sparkling sense it covers merry.

clue.text: Problem boarding public transport around outskirts of town

a passenger boarding gets inside the vehicle, so one word goes inside the other

a rub is a difficulty, as in 'there's the rub'

explanation.surface: Trouble getting on a bus that loops round the edge of town.
explanation.definitionFit: A residential district lying on the edge of a town or city is exactly its outskirts.

clue.text: Sell slips in fashion shops

indicators.note: in places one word inside the other
the first letter slips down to the back of the word

parts.note: ton means the fashion or the fashionable set
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: Shops looks like a plural noun for stores, but it is a verb: to shop someone is British slang for informing on them.
explanation.definitionFit: To betray someone to the authorities is to inform against them, which is the slang verb sense.

clue.text: Drifters wear oversized trousers

parts.note: found across the two words

clue.text: Rent reduction withdrawn, last in house leaves

clue.text: Animal — three letters — beginning with A

clue.text: Stars back on TV in a one off

clue.text: Environmentalists with prominence creating a stink

clue.text: Inhibitions about gift almost bewildered son

parts.note: pressie is informal British for a present
taken as written

clue.text: Any food that can be cured. (Turkey excluded)

TR is the international vehicle code for Turkey

explanation.surface: A note that any curable food is fine, except turkey.
explanation.walkthrough: Cured food suggests bacon or ham, and turkey the bird; here cured means healed and Turkey is the country code.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun this word means anything fit to be eaten, so any foodstuff.

clue.text: Part of bride's outfit? It'll arrive after June 30, and the rest apparently

parts.note: July 1, written JUL I with the Roman numeral one, follows June 30

explanation.definitionFit: A small close-fitting skullcap of the kind worn by Shakespeare's heroine is often worn by brides with a veil.

clue.text: Celtic hooligans due to leave Dundee's ground

explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland a young tearaway or lout is a ned, so the plural means Scottish yobs.

clue.text: More smart meters ultimately produce recipe to cut excess usage

taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: Smart meters reads as the home energy device; smart belongs with More and means neatly turned out.

clue.text: Summerhouse view that's amazing overlooking Yarmouth's front

parts.note: to gaze is to view

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Yarmouth

explanation.walkthrough: Overlooking sounds like having a view over the front, but it means disregarding a letter. Great Yarmouth is an English seaside town.

clue.text: Ant does this when first appearing, Dec starting late fails

definitions.text: Ant does this when first appearing

indicators.note: a late start means the opening letter is missing

parts.note: taken as written
to lose is to fail

explanation.surface: Ant and Dec, the British TV presenting duo, with Dec arriving late and flopping.
explanation.walkthrough: Ant and Dec are a famous British TV double act; here the ant is an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: An insect emerging from its pupa or egg is said to do this, the moment it first appears as an adult.

clue.text: Launch of newspaper, a vital year to come out

taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: Launch of newspaper reads as one phrase, but only Launch is the definition and of is part of the wordplay.

clue.text: Let off a bit of steam, but you've no right to swear

parts.note: to curse is to swear
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Venting your frustration is fine, but you have no right to use bad language.
explanation.walkthrough: Let off a bit of steam reads as one idiom, but Let off is the definition: to pardon.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a colloquial clipped form of excuse, meaning to pardon or let someone go unpunished.

clue.text: Meeting overran, I messed up somewhat

parts.note: found spanning these words

clue.text: Not hard to get to the answer

clue.text: Back in the shivering parts of December and January

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is singular in sense though worded as parts: one month spanning parts of both.

clue.text: Finishes off latte and exits after breaking cafe stools

clue.text: Collage is toneless to some extent, I'm not keen on the greys

clue.text: Scandinavians idolised these famed skiers regularly

clue.text: Monks pronounced Daniel's boast on leaving lion's den?
